newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong gears up for Tiananmen anniversary rally.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong gears up for Tiananmen anniversary rally.

text.p: Hong Kong's democracy movement geared up on Tuesday to mark the anniversary of China's bloody 1989 crackdown in the last big protest rally before Chinese rule is restored over the British colony.

In a park named after Britain's 19th century empress, Queen Victoria, democracy activists erected a controversial "Pillar of Shame" statue of twisted bodies symbolising oppression, ahead of the June 4 anniversary of Beijing's Tiananmen Square massacre.

Tanks of the People's Liberation Army, whose advance units have already arrived here, thundered into the square that night eight years ago and crushed a student-led pro-democracy campaign, with heavy loss of life.

Hong Kong people will pour into the park on Wednesday night to remember the bloodbath and its victims with a huge candlit vigil, an annual -- peaceful -- event drawing tens of thousands of sympathisers.
In 1989 a million people flooded Hong Kong's streets in an anti-Beijing outburst, including now-purged members of China's official organisations in Hong Kong, like Xinhua news agency.
China is taking back Hong Kong at midnight on June 30, ending 156 years of British colonial rule.
The capitalist metropolis of 6.4 million mostly-Chinese people will become a virtually autonomous part of China, allowed to keep its capitalist system for a further 50 years.

However, China and Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa are preparing to remove the elected legislature, install an appointed body instead and reduce political liberties introduced in the twilight years of British rule. On July 1 not one member of the new establishlment will have been elected by the people.

On Monday Tung said it was time to forget Tiananmen and he criticised the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements in China, the main organiser of pro- democracy protests, branded as subversive by Beijing.
Tung promised in a Hong Kong television interview there would be no crackdown on dissidents.
But he said: "As a member of the Chinese nation it's now time for everyone to put aside the baggage of June 4."
Last Sunday 3,500 people marched to China's mission in Hong Kong to demand a reversal of the "counter-revolutionary" verdict on Tiananmen, and the release of all political prisoners.
Han Dongfang, the best known Chinese dissident in Hong Kong, who led a free trade union in China in 1989, said authorities in Hong Kong were already showing opposition to the June 4 vigil.

"The pro-democratic people of Hong Kong will continue to go," Han said. "But the question is: how many people will continue to speak out without being afraid. Someone says something 2,000 km away and it frightens you."
He said Hong Kong people had faith in reformist Beijing before the crackdown, but in 1989 they lost their trust.
An opinion poll by Hong Kong University on Monday indicated 63.1 percent of people believed Beijing was wrong to suppress the 1989 movement, while 26.8 percent said they did not know.
However, only 35.8 percent of people believed the Beijing students were right to campaign for democracy, while 17.4 percent thought they were wrong, and 46.8 percent didn't know.
A resounding 75 percent however said Hong Kong people should push for democracy in China, and 55.8 percent said human rights would improve in China within three years.
The eight-metre-tall Pillar of Shame by Danish artist Jans Galschiot has sparked a row between democracy activists and local councils who refuse to put it on show at the handover.

As the Pillar was erected on Tuesday, another sculpture nearby conveyed the mixed end-of-empire sentiments. The bronze statue of Queen Victoria was recently restored after a mainland Chinese "artist" smashed in its nose with a hammer and covered the sculpture in red paint.
